questions.subtopic: 3A1 Running internal audit operations. Advice from the plan's reserve
questions.question: Under criteria agreed with the board, only dropping or delaying significant-risk work is a significant plan change. What is chief audit executive Rosa's BEST course when the logistics director seeks advice the reserve hours cover?

options.A: Raise it with the board and senior management as a conflicting demand
options.B: Use the reserve, once the board approves the change
options.C: Use the reserve, and report the advice in periodic results
options.D: Defer it to next year's plan after the risk assessment

questions.key_concept: Only significant plan changes need the board's approval; advice drawn from an approved reserve that displaces no significant-risk work is reported with other results.
questions.pre_read: Check what the agreed criteria call significant and whether anything planned is displaced before deciding who must approve.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.4 requires the board to approve the plan and significant changes to it; its considerations have the chief audit executive, the board and senior management agree what counts as significant, and have the plan reserve hours for ad hoc requests. This request uses that reserve and meets none of the agreed criteria, so no approval is needed. Standard 8.1 still has advice reported with other results. Option B treats every change as significant.

wrong_explanations.A: A conflicting demand is a clash, such as advice replacing planned assurance; this request displaces nothing, so there is no clash to report.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the board approves significant changes, but under the agreed criteria this request is not one, and the reserve it uses is already in the approved plan.
wrong_explanations.D: The plan is dynamic and the reserve exists for requests that arise during the year; deferring one it covers wastes hours the board approved.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a conflicting demand needs a clash, such as advice replacing planned assurance, and D, because the approved reserve exists for requests that arise during the year.
Final two: C beats B because the board approves only significant changes, and the agreed criteria put this request below that line.
Exam cue: on CIA plan-change questions, check the agreed significance criteria first; only a significant change needs the board's approval.

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Running internal audit operations. Training after rewritten methodologies
questions.question: A Moroccan phosphate group moves internal audit onto new software and absorbs a subsidiary's audit team; chief audit executive Youssef rewrites the methodologies to fit. Which step is Youssef MOST clearly required to take?

options.A: Train the internal auditors on the rewritten methodologies
options.B: Submit the rewritten methodologies to the board for approval
options.C: Post the rewritten manual in the software for auditors to read
options.D: Commission an external assessment before the new methods apply

questions.key_concept: The chief audit executive sets, evaluates and updates the methodologies and must train internal auditors on them; board approval attaches to other documents.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the chief audit executive owns from what the board approves, then ask which step is required rather than allowed.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.3 requires the chief audit executive to set methodologies, update them as needed after significant changes affecting the function (its considerations name new technology and a change in the team's size or makeup), and train internal auditors on them. Under Standard 6.3's essential conditions the board approves the charter, plan, budget and resource plan; no Standard requires board approval of methodologies, so option B adds a step.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the board approves the charter, the plan, the budget and the resource plan; methodologies are the chief audit executive's to set, update and train auditors on.
wrong_explanations.C: Making the manual available is not enough: Standard 9.3 requires the chief audit executive to give internal auditors training on the methodologies.
wrong_explanations.D: A merger of audit teams or a significant methodology change may justify an earlier external assessment under Standard 8.4, but none is required before use.

tips: Eliminate: C, because Standard 9.3 requires training, not just access to the manual, and D, because an earlier external assessment is an option, not a step required first.
Final two: A beats B because methodologies are the chief audit executive's to set and update; the board approves the charter, plan, budget and resource plan.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about the function's methods, the chief audit executive sets, updates and trains; board approval attaches to the charter, plan, budget and resource plan.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Managing money, people and technology. A budget that leaves out the strategy's training
questions.question: Chief audit executive Ana's draft budget for a Portuguese utility covers salaries, travel and software, leaving the data-skills training the strategy calls for to a later request. Which view of it is MOST accurate?

options.A: Complete: the data-skills training can follow in a separate request
options.B: Incomplete: it must hold a reserve for unforeseen plan changes
options.C: Complete, once the finance director reviews it under the budget process
options.D: Incomplete: it must include the data-skills training it leaves out

questions.key_concept: The budget must let the strategy be carried out and the plan achieved, training included; a reserve for unforeseen changes is optional.
questions.pre_read: Sort each element of a budget into what the chief audit executive must include and what the budget may hold.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 10.1 requires the chief audit executive to develop a budget that enables the strategy and the plan, and states that it includes what the function needs to operate, training and technology among them. Leaving training the strategy already names to a later request leaves the draft short. Its considerations say the budget may hold a reserve for unexpected but necessary plan changes (B): an option, not a gap.

wrong_explanations.A: A separate request suits needs nobody foresaw; training the strategy already calls for belongs in the budget the board approves.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Standard 10.1's considerations say the budget may hold a reserve for unexpected but necessary plan changes; that is optional, while training is required content.
wrong_explanations.C: Following the organization's budget process is good practice, but a review does not fill the gap: the draft still omits needs the strategy sets.

tips: Eliminate: A, because foreseen needs belong in the budget, not a later request, and C, because a finance review cannot complete a budget that omits the strategy's needs.
Final two: D beats B because Standard 10.1 makes training part of the budget, while a reserve for unexpected changes is optional.
Exam cue: on CIA budget questions, separate what the budget must contain from what it may hold; a missing optional item never makes a draft deficient.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Managing money, people and technology. Specialists assigned away from their work
questions.question: A Thai bank's audit function has two IT specialists and enough hours, yet chief audit executive Somchai staffs cash counts with them and cybersecurity work with generalists. What is MOST clearly unmet?

options.A: Staff who are appropriate in their mix of skills
options.B: Staff who are effectively deployed across engagements
options.C: Staff who are sufficient in number and hours
options.D: Staff limits reported to the board and senior management

questions.key_concept: Human resources must be appropriate (the right skills), sufficient (enough people and hours) and effectively deployed (assigned where they best achieve the plan).
questions.pre_read: Name which of the three human resources tests the facts already satisfy before choosing the one they fail.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 10.2 has the chief audit executive strive for human resources that are appropriate (the right blend of knowledge and skills), sufficient (enough people and hours) and effectively deployed (assigned where they best achieve the plan). Somchai's function has IT specialists and enough hours, so the first two tests are met; putting the specialists on cash counts while generalists take the cybersecurity work fails deployment. Option A blames a mix the function already has.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: appropriate means the function holds the right blend of knowledge and skills, and it has IT specialists; they are simply assigned to the wrong work.
wrong_explanations.C: Sufficient refers to the quantity of people and hours, and the stem says the function has enough hours for its plan.
wrong_explanations.D: Limits are reported when resources fall short of the plan; this function has the skills and hours, so there is no shortfall to report.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the function has enough hours, and D, because reporting limits applies to a shortfall, which this function does not have.
Final two: B beats A because the function has the IT skills; the gap lies in who is assigned to which engagement.
Exam cue: on CIA staffing questions, sort the problem: wrong skills is appropriateness, too few people is sufficiency, right people in the wrong places is deployment.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Managing money, people and technology. A team-wide gap analysis but no one assessed
questions.question: Okello, a Ugandan sugar producer's chief audit executive, runs a team-wide skills gap analysis, funds courses and gives review notes on workpapers. Which practice is Okello MOST clearly required to add?

options.A: A mentoring scheme pairing junior auditors with seniors
options.B: Bonuses tied to the function's strategic objectives
options.C: An evaluation of each internal auditor's competencies
options.D: A plan setting each auditor's yearly continuing education

questions.key_concept: The chief audit executive must evaluate each internal auditor's competencies; training, supervisory feedback and mentoring are alternative routes to develop them.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the chief audit executive already does with each practice, and ask which ones a requirement names and which only a consideration.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 10.2 requires the chief audit executive to evaluate each internal auditor's competencies and help them develop through training, supervisory feedback and/or mentoring. A team-wide gap analysis rates the function, not each person, and Standard 12.3's considerations note that assessing staff skills reaches beyond reviewing workpapers, so review notes do not fill the gap. Okello already trains and gives feedback, so mentoring (A) is optional.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: mentoring is one of the development routes Standard 10.2 lists with "and/or"; Okello already uses training and supervisory feedback, so it is optional here.
wrong_explanations.B: Standard 10.2's considerations say pay, promotion and recognition should support the strategic objectives; that is good practice, not a required step.
wrong_explanations.D: Standard 3.2's considerations say the chief audit executive should consider a continuing education plan; a should, while evaluating each auditor is a must.

tips: Eliminate: B, because rewards tied to strategy are a consideration, and D, because a continuing education plan is something the chief audit executive should consider, not a requirement.
Final two: C beats A because individual evaluation is required, while mentoring is one of three development routes that training and feedback already cover.
Exam cue: on CIA people-management questions, a team-wide analysis does not replace the required look at each internal auditor's competencies.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Managing money, people and technology. Tools never evaluated after purchase
questions.question: Chief audit executive Mette lists four technology practices of a Danish freight firm's internal audit function for its board. Which practice MOST clearly falls short of the Standards?

options.A: Audit software in use six years with no evaluation since purchase
options.B: Tool rollouts planned together with IT and information security
options.C: Tool funding requests put to the board and senior management
options.D: Analytics run on the risk function's system, not a separate audit one

questions.key_concept: The chief audit executive must evaluate the function's technology regularly and pursue improvements; sharing governance, risk and control systems with other departments is encouraged.
questions.pre_read: Test each practice against what Standard 10.3 requires or encourages before reacting to how independent it sounds.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 10.3 requires the chief audit executive to evaluate the function's technology regularly and pursue chances to improve effectiveness and efficiency; software in use for six years with no evaluation misses that. Its considerations encourage joining other departments in common governance, risk and control systems, so option D is good practice: running analytics on a shared system does not hand internal audit's judgment to the risk function.

wrong_explanations.B: Standard 10.3 requires the chief audit executive to collaborate with IT and information security when implementing technology, so this practice conforms.
wrong_explanations.C: Standard 10.3's considerations have well-supported technology funding requests presented to the board and senior management for approval, so this practice conforms.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: Standard 10.3's considerations encourage joining other departments in common governance, risk and control systems; using one does not by itself impair independence.

tips: Eliminate: B, because working with IT and information security is required, and C, because technology funding requests go to the board and senior management under Standard 10.3's considerations.
Final two: A beats D because regular evaluation of the function's technology is required, while a shared risk and control system is encouraged.
Exam cue: on CIA technology questions, tools already in use still need regular evaluation, and sharing a system with other departments is encouraged, not a threat to independence.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Internal audit strategy and its stakeholders. What the board does with the strategy
questions.question: Chief audit executive Aoife has drafted a four-year internal audit strategy for an Irish dairy cooperative, with a vision, objectives and initiatives. Which step do the Standards MOST clearly require for it?

options.A: Obtain the board's approval before carrying it out
options.B: Have senior management approve it and inform the board
options.C: Update it after each yearly documented risk assessment
options.D: Review it with the board and senior management periodically

questions.key_concept: The strategy is reviewed with the board and senior management periodically; the board approves the charter, plan, budget and resource plan, not the strategy.
questions.pre_read: Recall which documents the board approves and which it reviews, and read each option's verb closely.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.2 requires the chief audit executive to develop and carry out a strategy holding a vision, strategic objectives and supporting initiatives, and to review it with the board and senior management periodically. It asks for review, not approval. The board approves the charter, the plan and its significant changes, the budget and the resource plan. Option A borrows the plan's approval rule.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: board approval belongs to the charter, the internal audit plan, the budget and the resource plan; Standard 9.2 asks for periodic review of the strategy, not approval.
wrong_explanations.B: Senior management gives input and support and approves none of the function's key documents; the strategy is reviewed with the board, not just reported to it.
wrong_explanations.C: The yearly documented risk assessment is the internal audit plan's basis under Standard 9.4; the strategy is adjusted when objectives or expectations change.

tips: Eliminate: B, because senior management gives input and approves none of the function's key documents, and C, because the yearly risk assessment underpins the plan, not the strategy.
Final two: D beats A because Standard 9.2 requires periodic review with the board and senior management; approval is for the charter, plan, budget and resource plan.
Exam cue: on CIA strategy questions, watch the verb: the board approves the plan, but the strategy is reviewed with the board and senior management.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Internal audit strategy and its stakeholders. The missing middle of a strategy
questions.question: The draft internal audit strategy of an Argentine wine exporter holds a five-year vision and a dated list of initiatives on auditor skills and technology, and nothing else. What does the draft MOST need?

options.A: The year's engagements that will deliver each initiative
options.B: Strategic objectives setting achievable targets for the function
options.C: A mission statement to sit above the vision
options.D: A gap analysis of the function's current and desired states

questions.key_concept: A strategy must hold a vision, strategic objectives and supporting initiatives; a mission statement is common usage that the Standards do not require.
questions.pre_read: List the parts a strategy must contain and check each against the draft before weighing parts that are only customary.
questions.correct_explanation: Under Standard 9.2 the strategy must contain three parts: a vision, strategic objectives and the initiatives that support them. Its considerations describe the objectives as achievable targets for reaching the vision, with the initiatives as the steps for each. This draft lacks the middle element. A mission statement (C) is common usage: the Standards neither require nor define one, and the board-approved charter holds the binding mandate.

wrong_explanations.A: Engagements and hours belong in the internal audit plan under Standard 9.4; the strategy's initiatives are steps for the function itself, not engagements.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a mission statement is common usage; the Standards do not require one, while strategic objectives are a required part of the strategy.
wrong_explanations.D: Standard 9.2's considerations name a gap analysis as one way to develop a strategy; it is a method, not one of the strategy's required parts.

tips: Eliminate: A, because engagements belong to the plan, not the strategy, and D, because a gap analysis is one way to build a strategy, not one of its parts.
Final two: B beats C because strategic objectives are a required element of the strategy, while a mission statement is common usage the Standards do not require.
Exam cue: on CIA strategy questions, check for all three required parts: a vision, strategic objectives and supporting initiatives.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Internal audit strategy and its stakeholders. Skills the plan needs and the budget cannot buy
questions.question: Hana, chief audit executive of a Czech carmaker, finds no auditor has the skills for the plan's battery-plant assurance engagement, a strategic priority, and the budget cannot buy them. What is Hana's BEST response?

options.A: Tell the board the impact and propose ways to obtain the skills
options.B: Ask senior management to fund the skills outside the budget
options.C: Tell the board the impact and remove the engagement from the plan
options.D: Raise it at the board's yearly discussion of resource sufficiency

questions.key_concept: Short of resources, the chief audit executive must develop a way to obtain them and tell the board the impact and the remedy.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a shortfall obliges the chief audit executive to produce, and who decides any change to the approved plan.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 8.2 requires the chief audit executive to judge whether resources suffice for the mandate and plan and, if not, to work out how to obtain them and tell the board both the impact and the way the gap will be closed. Its considerations name options such as a guest auditor, training, hiring or an outside provider. Removing the engagement (C) skips that duty and makes a plan change only the board approves.

wrong_explanations.B: Senior management helps provide resources, but going to it alone bypasses the board, which approves the budget and must be told the impact and the remedy (Standard 8.2).
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: telling the board is required, but Standard 8.2 also requires a strategy to obtain resources, and dropping a planned engagement is a change the board approves.
wrong_explanations.D: The yearly discussion of resource sufficiency is a minimum; a shortfall that blocks a planned engagement is raised timely, not held for the routine meeting.

tips: Eliminate: B, because going to senior management alone bypasses the board, which approves the budget, and D, because a shortfall blocking planned work is raised timely, not saved for the yearly discussion.
Final two: A beats C because the chief audit executive must work out how to obtain the resources; dropping planned work is the board's decision.
Exam cue: on CIA resource questions, the chief audit executive brings the board both the impact and a way to close the gap.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Internal audit strategy and its stakeholders. An event that reopens the strategy
questions.question: Midway through a five-year internal audit strategy at a Norwegian salmon farmer, which event should MOST prompt chief audit executive Ingrid to bring the strategy's scheduled review forward?

options.A: Two of the function's six auditors resign and are replaced
options.B: An engagement finds a significant new fraud risk in exports
options.C: A new group president and two new directors take office
options.D: Management misses the due dates on three action plans

questions.key_concept: The strategy follows the organization's strategy, rules, leaders and quality results; new risks change the internal audit plan instead.
questions.pre_read: Match each event to what it changes: the strategy, the plan, the methodologies or follow-up of action plans.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.2's considerations say the strategy should be adjusted when the organization's strategic objectives or stakeholders' expectations change, and list events that may prompt an earlier review: a new organizational strategy or risk maturity, new policies or laws, changes in the board, senior management or the chief audit executive, and quality assessment results. New leaders bring new expectations. A new fraud risk (B) updates the plan.

wrong_explanations.A: Turnover may prompt a methodology review (Standard 9.3) or an earlier external assessment (Standard 8.4); the strategy's prompts name new board members, senior managers or a new chief audit executive.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a significant new risk calls for a timely update of the internal audit plan under Standard 9.4, not a review of the function's long-term strategy.
wrong_explanations.D: Missed action plan dates call for follow-up and, where needed, escalation under Standard 15.2; they concern management's actions, not the function's strategy.

tips: Eliminate: A, because staff turnover prompts a methodology review, not a strategy review, and D, because missed action plan dates lead to follow-up and escalation.
Final two: C beats B because new leaders change stakeholders' expectations, which the strategy follows, while a new risk changes the plan.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, the strategy moves with the organization's strategy, rules and leaders; the plan moves with risks.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Chief audit executive reporting and relationships. News the agreed report format leaves out
questions.question: Chief audit executive Elif learns regulators are probing a Turkish bank's anti-money-laundering program; the report format the board agreed omits the topic, and management has not told the board. What is Elif's BEST course?

options.A: Ask senior management to decide whether the board should hear it
options.B: Report it to the board once the agreed format covers it
options.C: Report it to the board after an engagement confirms the facts
options.D: Report it to the board, although the agreed format omits it

questions.key_concept: The chief audit executive must give the board what it needs for oversight, including what the chief audit executive judges valuable beyond any agreed format.
questions.pre_read: Separate the duty to inform the board from the agreed arrangements for how reports look and how often they come.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 8.1 requires the chief audit executive to give the board the information it needs for oversight, whether the board asked for it or the chief audit executive judges it valuable. A regulatory inquiry the board has not heard of is such information. Confirming the format with the board periodically is a consideration that serves the board; it does not limit what must be reported, so waiting for a revised format (B) fails the duty.

wrong_explanations.A: Board communications are coordinated with senior management under Standard 6.3, but coordination is not permission; senior management does not decide what the board hears.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: revising the format with the board is good practice, but Standard 8.1 also covers information the chief audit executive judges valuable, so the report cannot wait for it.
wrong_explanations.C: An engagement on the program may follow, but the board needs to know of the inquiry now to carry out its oversight, not after the fieldwork.

tips: Eliminate: A, because coordinating with senior management does not let it decide what the board hears, and C, because an engagement would delay information the board needs now.
Final two: D beats B because the duty to inform the board covers what the chief audit executive judges valuable, beyond any agreed format.
Exam cue: on CIA board-reporting questions, the agreed format is a floor, not a ceiling; the chief audit executive adds what the board needs for oversight.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Chief audit executive reporting and relationships. An urgent change before the board meets
questions.question: Floods force chief audit executive Ayesha to move auditors to emergency-payment assurance at once, postponing a payroll audit, significant under the agreed criteria; the board cannot meet for eight weeks. What is Ayesha's BEST course?

options.A: Wait for the board's approval at its meeting before moving staff
options.B: Inform the board immediately and seek formal approval soon after
options.C: Move the staff and report the change in the year-end summary
options.D: Have senior management approve the move and inform the board later

questions.key_concept: Significant plan changes need board approval; when a risk cannot wait for the next meeting, the board is told immediately and approves soon after.
questions.pre_read: Check whether the change is significant, then whether the risk can wait for the next board meeting.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.4 requires board approval of the plan and its significant changes, which the chief audit executive discusses with the board and senior management. For a risk that cannot wait for the board's next discussion, its considerations (a should) set a protocol: tell the board at once, then get formal approval at the earliest opportunity. Waiting eight weeks (A) leaves the flood payments without assurance and adds nothing prompt notice does not.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: board approval is required, but when a risk cannot wait, Standard 9.4's considerations have the board told at once and approval given soon after.
wrong_explanations.C: A significant change needs the board's approval; reporting it months later in a summary leaves the board approving nothing.
wrong_explanations.D: Senior management gives input on the plan but does not approve it or its significant changes; that approval is the board's.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a significant change needs board approval, not a later summary, and D, because senior management gives input but does not approve plan changes.
Final two: B beats A because an urgent significant change is told to the board at once and approved formally as soon as possible, rather than delayed.
Exam cue: on CIA plan-change questions, urgency changes the timing, never the approver: the board still approves, as soon as it can.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Chief audit executive reporting and relationships. A chief executive who wants a planned audit dropped
questions.question: A Mexican retailer's chief executive tells chief audit executive Diego to drop planned assurance over a new, high-risk e-commerce platform; their talks have not resolved it. What is Diego's BEST course?

options.A: Give the board the facts and circumstances of the dispute
options.B: Treat it as senior management accepting risk beyond appetite
options.C: Drop it and tell the board why a high-risk area lacks assurance
options.D: Record the instruction as a scope limitation in the final communication

questions.key_concept: A disagreement with senior management that may hamper internal audit's work goes to the board as facts; the board approves dropping planned work.
questions.pre_read: Identify who can change the approved plan, and what the chief audit executive owes the board when senior management blocks the work.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 8.1 requires the chief audit executive, when a disagreement with senior management may hamper the function in doing its work, to give the board the facts and circumstances so it can consider intervening. Dropping a planned high-risk engagement is also a significant plan change, which Standard 9.4 leaves to the board. Option C drops the work first, on the chief executive's word.

wrong_explanations.B: Standard 11.5's route is for risk that management accepts above appetite or tolerance; here the dispute is over internal audit's own work, which Standard 8.1 sends to the board.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: Standard 9.4 does require explaining why a high-risk area lacks assurance, but dropping a planned engagement is a significant change the board approves, not the chief executive.
wrong_explanations.D: A scope limitation is disclosed in the final communication of an engagement that ran; here the whole engagement is at stake before it starts.

tips: Eliminate: B, because risk acceptance concerns management's response to a risk, not a dispute over audit work, and D, because a scope limitation note comes too late for an engagement not yet started.
Final two: A beats C because the chief executive cannot remove a planned engagement; the board approves significant changes and decides whether to intervene.
Exam cue: on CIA questions where senior management blocks internal audit's work, the chief audit executive gives the board the facts; the board decides.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Chief audit executive reporting and relationships. One root cause across five engagements
questions.question: Five engagements at an Indonesian palm-oil group, each with its own final communication, traced findings to one root cause: estate managers approving their own purchase orders. What is chief audit executive Wayan's BEST next step?

options.A: Plan a group-wide audit next year with the board and senior management
options.B: Give an overall conclusion on the group's purchasing controls
options.C: Report the shared cause, with advice, to the board and senior management
options.D: Reissue the five final communications with the shared cause added

questions.key_concept: Themes across engagements, such as a shared root cause, must reach the board and senior management timely with insights, advice or conclusions.
questions.pre_read: Look past each engagement to the pattern, then ask what must happen now and what only may follow later.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 11.3 requires the chief audit executive, on identifying themes such as a root cause shared across engagements, to communicate them timely to the board and senior management, with insights, advice or conclusions. Its considerations add that a theme may lead to more engagements across the organization, so a group-wide engagement (A) may follow, but it does not replace telling the board and senior management now.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Standard 11.3's considerations note a theme may lead to more engagements, but planning one is not reporting the theme, which must reach the board and senior management timely.
wrong_explanations.B: An organization-level conclusion is made when law, industry rules or stakeholders call for one, none of which the stem names; the duty triggered here is reporting the theme.
wrong_explanations.D: Standard 11.4's corrections are for significant errors or omissions in a final communication; each of these was right for its own engagement.

tips: Eliminate: B, because an organization-level conclusion is given when required, with criteria and scope, and D, because reissuing is for significant errors, which these communications do not contain.
Final two: C beats A because a theme must be communicated timely with advice; a later engagement may follow but cannot stand in for it.
Exam cue: on CIA questions where one cause recurs across engagements, the chief audit executive reports the theme to the board and senior management promptly.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Chief audit executive reporting and relationships. A required overall conclusion with no scope
questions.question: Required by regulators to conclude yearly on a Saudi bank's internal control, chief audit executive Faisal drafts one naming the request, criteria and supporting engagements, relying on no other provider. What does it MOST need?

options.A: Each engagement's rating alongside its findings
options.B: The scope, with its limitations and the period covered
options.C: Senior management's written agreement with the conclusion
options.D: A disclosure that no other provider's work was relied on

questions.key_concept: An organization-level conclusion states the request, criteria, scope with limitations and period, supporting information, and any reliance on other assurance providers.
questions.pre_read: List the elements a required overall conclusion must state, then tick off what the draft already has and what the facts make unnecessary.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 11.3 sets what an organization-level conclusion must state when communicated: what was asked for, the criteria used, the scope with its limits and the period it covers, the information behind it in summary, and any reliance on other assurance providers. Faisal's draft lacks the scope and period. Reliance is disclosed only when it exists (D), and here none does.

wrong_explanations.A: The conclusion summarizes the information behind it; it need not repeat each engagement's rating and findings, which went out in each final communication.
wrong_explanations.C: The conclusion reflects the chief audit executive's professional judgment; management's agreement is not one of the elements Standard 11.3 requires.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: Standard 11.3 requires disclosing reliance on other assurance providers if there is any; with none, the required element still missing is the scope and period.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a summary of the supporting information is enough, and C, because the conclusion is the chief audit executive's judgment, not a document management signs.
Final two: B beats D because the scope and period are always required, while reliance is disclosed only when another provider's work was used.
Exam cue: on CIA overall-conclusion questions, check the required elements: request, criteria, scope and period, supporting information, and any reliance.
